exact_citation: Rame Gowda (Dead) by LRs v. M. Varadappa Naidu, (2004) 1 SCC 769
supporting_passage: A person in peaceful settled possession is entitled to retain it and cannot be dispossessed even by the true owner without due process of law.
contradiction_or_limit: Applies only to settled possession, not stray or casual trespass.
text: Rame Gowda v. M. Varadappa Naidu, (2004) 1 SCC 769. Settled possession. If a person is in peaceful, settled possession of property, the rightful owner cannot take the law into their own hands and evict them forcibly. Relief under Section 6 of Specific Relief Act 1963 applies.

exact_citation: Krishna Ram Mahale (Dead) by LRs v. Mrs. Shobha Venkat Rao, (1989) 4 SCC 131
supporting_passage: Even a trespasser or occupant with expired license in settled possession cannot be dispossessed without due course of law.
contradiction_or_limit: Does not confer title to the occupant, merely protects from extra-judicial force.
text: Krishna Ram Mahale v. Mrs. Shobha Venkat Rao, (1989) 4 SCC 131. Illegal dispossession. Unlawful eviction by force is forbidden under Indian jurisprudence. Possession must be recovered through civil court process.

exact_citation: Ravinder Kaur Grewal v. Manjit Kaur, (2019) 8 SCC 729
supporting_passage: A person who has perfected title by adverse possession over 12 continuous hostile years can use it as a sword to file a suit for declaration of title, not just as a shield.
contradiction_or_limit: Overrules earlier narrow precedents that restricted adverse possession only to defendants.
text: Ravinder Kaur Grewal v. Manjit Kaur, (2019) 8 SCC 729. Adverse possession can be used affirmatively by a plaintiff under Article 65 of Limitation Act 1963 for declaration of ownership after uninterrupted 12 years of hostile possession.

exact_citation: Hemaji Waghaji Jat v. Bhikhabhai Khengarbhai Harijan, (2009) 16 SCC 517
supporting_passage: Heavy burden of proof lies on claimant of adverse possession. Possession must be nec vi, nec clam, nec precario (without force, without secrecy, without permission).
contradiction_or_limit: Judicial criticism of adverse possession as encouraging land grabbing, requiring strict compliance.
text: Hemaji Waghaji Jat v. Bhikhabhai, (2009) 16 SCC 517. Requirements for adverse possession under Limitation Act Article 65: clear, open, hostile, continuous possession for 12 years. Strict standard of evidence.

exact_citation: Suraj Lamp & Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. State of Haryana, (2012) 1 SCC 656
supporting_passage: Transfer of immovable property can only be effected by a registered sale deed. GPA, SA, or will transactions do not convey ownership.
contradiction_or_limit: Does not invalidate genuine development agreements or statutory Section 53A part-performance.
text: Suraj Lamp & Industries v. State of Haryana, (2012) 1 SCC 656. Power of Attorney sales. Immovable property sales require registered instrument under Section 17 of Registration Act 1908. Unregistered agreements do not transfer title.

exact_citation: Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh, (2020) 2 SCC 569
supporting_passage: The State cannot claim adverse possession against its own citizens whose land was taken without due process. Right to property is a constitutional and human right.
contradiction_or_limit: Specifically bars governmental encroachment under the guise of adverse possession.
text: Vidya Devi v. State of Himachal Pradesh, (2020) 2 SCC 569. Article 300A property protection. State taking private land without compensation or procedure cannot claim adverse possession.

exact_citation: P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma, (2007) 6 SCC 59
supporting_passage: Animus possidendi (intent to possess adversely) is essential. Permissive possession, no matter how long, cannot mature into adverse title.
contradiction_or_limit: Permissive or family arrangement cannot be treated as adverse without explicit ouster.
text: P.T. Munichikkanna Reddy v. Revamma, (2007) 6 SCC 59. Animus possidendi. Continuous possession without hostile animus against rightful owner does not create adverse possession.

exact_citation: Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, (2004) 10 SCC 779
supporting_passage: Pleadings in adverse possession must state exact inception date, nature of possession, and how open knowledge reached the true owner.
contradiction_or_limit: Vague claims lacking precise start dates are liable to be dismissed on pleadings.
text: Karnataka Board of Wakf v. Government of India, (2004) 10 SCC 779. Adverse possession pleading standards. Claimant must demonstrate exactly when and how hostile possession began.

exact_citation: Nair Service Society Ltd v. K.C. Alexander, AIR 1968 SC 1165
supporting_passage: Possessory title is good against all the world except the true owner. Even outside 6 months of Section 6, prior peaceful possession can support ejectment of a subsequent trespasser.
contradiction_or_limit: Defeated if the defendant proves superior title.
text: Nair Service Society Ltd v. K.C. Alexander, AIR 1968 SC 1165. Possessory title. Prior possession gives right against any subsequent interloper or trespasser lacking title.

exact_citation: Maria Margarida Sequeria Fernandes v. Erasmo Jack de Sequeria, (2012) 5 SCC 370
supporting_passage: Caretakers, guests, or employees do not acquire settled possession against the owner. Due process requires a fair opportunity to be heard, not protracted obstruction.
contradiction_or_limit: Limits claims of settled possession by servants, agents, and permissive occupiers.
text: Maria Margarida Sequeria Fernandes v. Erasmo Jack de Sequeria, (2012) 5 SCC 370. Due process in property disputes. Caretakers and licensees have no possessory rights against the true owner.

exact_citation: Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy, (2008) 4 SCC 594
supporting_passage: Where title is disputed or under a cloud, a mere suit for permanent injunction is not maintainable; plaintiff must seek declaration of title and possession.
contradiction_or_limit: Pure injunction suits maintainable only when title is undisputed and plaintiff is in clear possession.
text: Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy, (2008) 4 SCC 594. Suit for declaration vs injunction. If plaintiff's title is under a serious cloud, declaration of title is mandatory.

exact_citation: State of Haryana v. Mukesh Kumar, (2011) 10 SCC 404
supporting_passage: Reiterated strict skepticism toward adverse possession claims and urged reform of archaic squatter laws.
contradiction_or_limit: Demonstrates judicial reluctance to grant adverse possession without unimpeachable proof.
text: State of Haryana v. Mukesh Kumar, (2011) 10 SCC 404. Severe judicial condemnation of adverse possession without documented legal entitlement.

supporting_passage: Suit by person dispossessed of immovable property without consent otherwise than in due course of law. Limitation period is 6 months from dispossession.
contradiction_or_limit: Cannot be instituted against the Government. No appeal or review lies from any order under this section.
text: Section 6 of Specific Relief Act 1963. Fast track remedy for illegal dispossession within 6 months. Focuses exclusively on prior possession, not legal title. Unappealable order.

supporting_passage: Admissibility of electronic records requires dual-signatory certificate (custodian of device and technical expert) with SHA hash values.
contradiction_or_limit: Applies to events on or after 1 July 2024; pre-2024 electronic records governed by IEA Section 65B.
text: Section 63 BSA 2023. Mandatory certification for secondary electronic records (WhatsApp audio, CCTV footage, mobile video) requiring dual signatures and cryptographic hash value.

supporting_passage: Criminal trespass: entering into or upon property in possession of another with intent to commit an offence or intimidate, insult or annoy.
text: Section 329 BNS 2023. Criminal trespass and house trespass. Applies to unlawful encroachment, broken locks, or forcible entry into disputed property.
